title: Hydrophobic 1-octadecanethiol functionalized copper catalyst promotes robust high-current CO2 gas-diffusion electrolysis
abstract: The electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 presents a promising strategy in addressing environmental and energy crisis. Significant progress has been achieved via CO2 gas diffusion electrolysis, to react at high selectivity and high rate. However, the gas diffusion layer (GDL) of the gas diffusion electrode (GDE) still suffers from low tolerance and limited active sites. Here, the hydrophobic 1-octadecanethiol molecular was functionalized over the Cu catalyst layer of the GDE, which simultaneously stabilizes the GDL and exposes abundant active solid–liquid–gas three-phase interfaces. The resultant GDE exhibits multi-carbon (C2+) product selectivity over faradaic efficiency (FE) of 70.0% in the range of 100 to 800 mA·cm, with the peak FEC2+ of 85.2% at 800 mA·cm . Notably, the strengthened GDE could continuously drive high-current electrolysis for more than 100 h without flooding. This work opens a new way to improve CO2 gas diffusion electrolysis via surface molecular engineering.

KEYWORDS CO2 reduction reaction, gas diffusion electrolysis, multi-carbon products, molecular engineering, hydrophobicity

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
The electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) driven by renewable electricity provides a sustainable route to shift chemical production away from fossil fuels [1–3]. In the past decades, significant progresses have been achieved over copper-based electrocatalysts to efficiently convert CO2 into multi-carbon (C2+) fuels and chemicals via catalyst design [4–10]. Unfortunately, the performance of the developed catalysts is limited by low solubility (33 mM at room temperature) and slow diffusion of CO2 if evaluated in the H-type cell that cannot deliver high-current CO2RR [11–13]; therefore, the flow cell configurations equipped with gas diffusion electrodes (GDEs) have been applied to alleviate the CO2 mass transport limitations [14, 15]. The GDE typically consists of a porous gas diffusion layer (GDL) capable of allowing gas transport but limiting liquid transport [16, 17]. However, the GDL suffers from extremely poor stability in the real CO2 gas diffusion electrolysis, and will be flooded with liquid filled in the pores which blocks CO2 to reach the active sites and increases its diffusion length, ultimately leading to the permanent inactivation of the GDEs [18–20]. It is still challenging to improve the lifetime of GDEs in the growing field of CO2 gas diffusion electrolysis.
Increasing the thickness of polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) coated microporous layers (MPLs) or directly using pure fibrous PTFE as GDL can reinforce the GDL to avoid the rapid flooding
of the GDEs, which might affect the catalytic selectivity and activity [21, 22]. Besides strengthening the GDL, continuously growing attentions have been paid to the modification of catalyst layer over the GDL [23, 24], that can regulate the microenvironment around the catalytic sites, simultaneously to improve the activity and stability of CO2 gas diffusion electrolysis. For instance, the hydrophobic nanoparticles were blended inside or over the catalyst layer which reduced the CO2 gas diffusion length and protected the GDL from flooding [25]. However, these efforts via adding hydrophobic additives could not roundly modify the catalyst surface. Recently, Wakerley developed a novel molecular engineering strategy over the flat Cu foil to modify the electrode hydrophobicity [12]. Inspired by this, we anticipate the hydrophobic functionalization over the catalytic sites at molecular or atomic scale will also be a breakthrough in the CO2 gas diffusion electrolysis, not only to concentrate CO2 gas for constructing abundant solid–liquid–gas three-phase interfaces but also to effectively protect GDL from flooding, which has never been reported, to the best of our knowledge.
With this in mind, we developed a hydrophobic molecular engineering strategy over the catalyst layer of the GDE to promote the CO2 gas diffusion electrolysis. For proof-of-concept, we electrodeposited classical hierarchically structured Cu dendrites as catalyst layers over the GDL (all the GDL model was used of H14C9 if not mentioned afterwards), and further

modified the catalyst surface with a monolayer of waxy alkanethiol. The resultant GDE exhibits high C2+ selectivity (mainly ethylene and ethanol) over a wide current density (j) ranging from 100 to 800 mA·cm−2, with the peak FEC2+ of 85.2% ± 5.7% (FEC2H4 of 35.5% ± 3.3% and FEC2H5OH of 38.0% ± 6.8%) at the j of 800 mA·cm−2, which is among the best of the reported Cu-based CO2RR catalysts. Notably, the GDE with a stable GDL model of Sigracet 28 BC could continuously drive the electrolysis for more than 100 h without obvious flooding. Our spectroscopic and electron microscopic results unambiguously demonstrate the robust existence of alkanethiol during the electrolysis, which could reduce the CO2 gas diffusion length and protect GDL from permanently flooding, leading to a sharp increase in both activity and stability.

sections.heading: 2.1 Catalyst layer fabrication
sections.text: The pristine GDE with dendritic Cu as catalyst layer was prepared by the galvanostatic electrodeposition. The electrodeposition solution consisted of 1.5 M H2SO4, 0.20 M CuSO4, 10 mM EDTA disodium and 10 mM PVP. Before starting electrodeposition, the GDL was soaked in electrodeposition solution for few minutes to reduce the surface hydrophobicity. The electrodeposition was undertaken in a three-electrode system by applying a current of −2 A for 40 s to the GDL with an actual size of 1.4 cm × 1.4 cm immersed in the 50 mL electrodeposition solution. Then the GDE was rinsed under a gentle stream of water followed immediately by being dried in vacuum oven at 60 °C to avoid oxidation.

sections.heading: 2.2 Hydrophobic molecular treatment
sections.text: The hydrophobic GDE was obtained by soaking the pristine GDE in 1-octadecanethiol solution for 20 min at 60 °C. Next, the GDE was submerged in ethylacetate for 5 min at 60 °C to remove extra 1-octadecanethiol on GDE and then dried directly in the air. It needs to be noted that the electrodeposition solution and 1-octadecanethiol must be changed after finishing no more than two pieces of GDE before starting another treatment.

sections.heading: 2.3 Characterizations
sections.text:
A Hitachi S4800 scanning electron microscope (SEM) was used to obtain the information of samples’ morphologies. Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) characterization was performed using ThermoFisher Talos F200X. High angle annular dark field (HAADF)-STEM images were recorded using a convergence semi angle of 11 mrad, and inner and outer collection angles of 59 and 200 mrad, respectively. Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) was carried out using 4 in-column Super-X detectors. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were carried out on Thermo ESCALAB 250Xi using Al Kα X-ray radiation (1,486.6 eV) for excitation. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were recorded on a Rigaku Ultima IV diffractometer using copper Kα radiation (40 kV, 30 mA) with a scan rate of 4 °·min−1. The gas adsorption isotherms of CO2 were measured at 25 °C with Micromeritics ASAP 2460. A Nicolet is 50 Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectrometer with ATR was used to analyze the surface information of catalysts. Ex situ X-ray absorption spectra at Cu K-edge on catalysts and standard references were collected at the beamline of 1W1B from Beijing synchrotron radiation facility, China. Cu foil, Cu2O and CuO were used as referenced samples. The electron storage ring was operated at 2.5 GeV with an average current of 200 mA. The data of absorption
were recorded in fluorescence mode. The acquired data were processed according to the standard procedures with the ATHENA module implemented in the IFEFFIT software packages. The normalized extended X-ray absorption fine-structure spectroscopy (EXAFS) was converted from energy to K-space and weighted by k3, and then was Fourier transformed to R-space. The contact angles were tested using a contact angle system (JC2000D3, Shanghai Zhongchen Digital Technology Apparatus Co., Ltd.) at ambient temperature, with the probe liquid being about 5 μL of water. All contact angle images were taken after the water droplet dropped on the surface of GDE for 15 min.

sections.heading: 3.1 The structure characterization of GDE
sections.text:
As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), the traditional GDE consists of a carbon fiber paper (CFP) as the supporting material, a MPL as the hydrophobic layer, and a catalyst layer over the MPL. In this configuration, the active solid–liquid–gas three-phase interface only exists between the MPL and the catalyst layer, and the CO2 transport would also be limited inside the catalyst layer. Nevertheless, the MPL would also be wetted or even flooded during the CO2 gas diffusion electrolysis, permanently losing the function of maintaining three-phase interface. In comparison, the hydrophobic molecular engineered catalyst layer over the GDL would expand the active three-phase interfaces into the catalyst layer, and supply the robust hydrophobic catalyst layer to prevent the MPL from flooding (Fig. 1(b)).
Inspired by this, we firstly electrodeposited a classic Cu dendrite catalyst layer over the MPL as pristine GDE (P-GDE).

Furthermore, 1-octadecanethiol molecules with long-chain alkane were chosen as a typical hydrophobic layer on the surface of GDE. Due to the sulfurization ability of sulfhydryl, the 1-octadecanethiol molecules could arrange on the metal surface with chemical absorption by forming bonding between S and substrate materials, and the long-chain alkanes of 1-octadecanethiol would play a hydrophobic role on the surface of GDE [12, 26–28]. The hydrophobic molecular treatment was carried out by immersing the P-GDE into the liquid 1-octadecanethiol to obtain the hydrophobic catalyst layer (H-GDE). As expected, the P-GDE would be easily flooded biased at the constant j of 500 mA·cm−2, showing a wildly fluctuating chronopotentiometric curve (Fig. 1(c)). For comparison, the modified H-GDE could deliver j of 500 mA·cm−2 at a relatively low and stable biased potential, indicating the obvious increased activity and stability after hydrophobic treatment.
The digital photo of H-GDE shows that the Cu catalyst layer was uniformly electrodeposited onto the GDE which features the good electrode flexibility (Fig. 2(a)). The contact angle measurements indicate that the H-GDE possesses an enduring superhydrophobicity, showing a contact angle of 150.4° (Fig. 2(b), left) and even after electrolysis for over 40 h (Fig. S1 in the Electronic Supplementary Material (ESM)), the H-GDE still maintains its hydrophobicity with a contact angle of 134.5° (Fig. 2(b), right). For comparison, the P-GDE exhibits a smaller contact angle of 59° (Fig. S2 in the ESM). The SEM images show that both of P-GDE and H-GDE exhibit a dendritic morphology (Fig. 2(c) and Figs. S3 and S4 in the ESM), which indicates that the surface molecular functionalization would not affect the morphology, decoupling the morphology effects to further study the hydrophobic molecular effects on the CO2 gas diffusion electrolysis. The SEM image of H-GDE after electrolysis also confirms the stability of morphological structure (Fig. S5 in the ESM).
The high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images of both H-GDE and P-GDE show the same characteristic lattice distance of 0.21 nm (Figs. S6 and S7 in the ESM), which is attributed to Cu(111), while the Cu of H-GDE is coated with an amorphous layer in a thickness of ~ 2.1 nm,
in coincidence with the chain-length of 1-octadecanethiol molecules bound upright [12] (from surface bounded S to the terminal C). STEM was further conducted to gather detailed structure information of the catalyst layer. In Fig. S8(a) in the ESM, the high-angle annular dark field-STEM (HAADF-STEM) image of H-GDE displays the intact dendrite morphology of Cu. The corresponding EDS elemental maps (Fig. S8(b) in the ESM) also suggest the Cu, C and S are homogeneously dispersed in the H-GDE, which confirms the existence of the alkanethiol layer. The HRTEM image of H-GDE after electrolysis further confirms an alkanethiol layer with a thickness of ~ 2.1 nm firmly anchoring on the Cu catalyst surface (Fig. S9 in the ESM). Notably, the HAADF-STEM image and corresponding EDS maps after electrolysis suggest the uniform coating of 1-ocadecanethiol over the catalyst layer (Fig. 2(d) in the ESM).
XRD analysis was further carried out (Fig. 2(e)), which confirms the existence of metallic Cu, along with the diffraction peak in the range of 20° to 30° indexed to the CFP. The XRD patterns collected after electrolysis show the same crystalline structures (Fig. S10 in the ESM). FTIR spectroscopy was further performed (Fig. 2(f)) to clarify the two characteristic peaks at 2,846 and 2,914 cm−1, which are assigned to methylene groups [29, 30], proving the presence of alkanethiol layer on the H-GDE. The FTIR spectrum of H-GDE after reaction testifies the presence of methylene groups (Fig. S11 in the ESM). In Fig. 2(g), the H-GDE also features the characteristic peak centered at 162.3 eV in the XPS result of S 2p region compared to the P-GDE, which is assigned to the Cu–S bonds [30, 31]. The XPS spectrum of H-GDE after electrolysis also shows presence of Cu–S bonds (Fig. S12 in the ESM). The cross-sectional scanning electron microscopic image and corresponding mappings indicate the uniform distribution of S elements over the catalyst layer (Fig. S13 in the ESM). The above mentioned results unambiguously demonstrate the hydrophobic 1-octadecanethiol molecules are functionalized over the Cu catalyst layer of the GDE, which is robust during CO2RR to endow the GDE with superhydrophobic.
Additional XPS analysis was conducted to reveal the valence states of Cu. Before the molecular treatment, the P-GDE shows obvious peaks at 934.5 and 954.6 eV in the Cu 2p region (Fig. S14 in the ESM), which are assigned to the Cu2+ species resulting from surface oxidation of CuO [6, 32, 33]. The H-GDE exhibits the decreased Cu oxidation states, especially in the Cu2+ peak intensity, indicating that the Cu2+ environments were removed to form Cu–S bonds. The Auger Cu LMM spectrum of H-GDE further proves the removal of Cu2+ of surface CuO (Fig. S15 in the ESM). The XPS spectrum after electrolysis exhibits no obvious discrepancy between pristine and postreaction electrodes (Fig. S16 in the ESM). In Fig. S17 in the ESM, the CO2 gas adsorption isotherms exhibit no obvious changes between P-GDE and H-GDE, which suggests that the alkanethiol layer would not affect the ability of CO2 adsorption.
The X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectra were collected to investigate the bulk oxidation states of catalyst layers. In Fig. S18 in the ESM, both P-GDE and H-GDE exhibit similar XANES spectra as Cu foil reference, which illustrates the major existence of metallic Cu, consistent with XRD results. The extended X-ray adsorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra demonstrate the similar coordination numbers of Cu–Cu between P-GDE and H-GDE (9.3 vs. 9.0), which is lower than the Cu foil reference (Fig. S19 and Table S1 in the ESM) [34]. The XAENS and EXAFS spectra of Cu K-edge for H-GDE collected after electrolysis exhibit no obvious difference with Cu foil reference (Figs. S18 and S19 and Table S1 in the ESM). Taken these results together, we illustrate the hydrophobic

sections.heading: 3.2 The electrocatalytic performance measurements of GDE
sections.text:
The home-made flow cell configuration was used to evaluate the performance in 1.0 M KOH electrolyte (Fig. S20 in the ESM). The linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves show that the j of H-GDE is lower than P-GDE at the low potential range due to the hydrophobicity (inset of Fig. 3(a)). As the potential increases, the j of H-GDE becomes obviously higher than that of P-GDE due to the electrowetting effect (Fig. 3(a)) [16, 35]. The initial capacitance measurements suggest the H-GDE initially owns a lower electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) than the P-GDE after functionalization (Fig. 3(b) and Figs. S21 and S22(a) in the ESM). However, the ECSA of H-GDE would increase during the CO2RR test (Figs. S22 and S23 in the ESM), suggesting that the pristine ECSA loss might result from the captured CO2 on the catalyst surface which reduces the contact of the electrolyte, instead of the decrease in geometric area after 1-ocadecanethiol treatment [12]. The electrochemical impedance spectroscopies (EIS) reveal the same tendency of increased charge transfer resistance along with the continuous electrolysis (Fig. S24 in the ESM). The time-dependent ECSA and EIS changes are ascribed to that the surface of the initial hydrophobic catalyst layer would be submerged by the electrolyte after electrolysis because of the electrowetting effect [18, 36] and possible loss of alkanethiol [12], thus increasing the catalytic current density.
Controlled current electrolysis was undertaken to collect and evaluate the product distribution. Gas chromatography (GC) and 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) were used to analyze the gaseous and liquid products (Fig. S25 in the ESM),
respectively. In Fig. 3(c) and Table S2 in the ESM, the H-GDE after hydrophobic treatment could steadily deliver j in the wide range from 100 to 800 mA·cm−2, showing the peak FEC2+ of 85.2% at the j of 800 mA·cm−2 with main C2+ products of C2H4 (35.5% ± 3.3%) and C2H5OH (38.0% ± 6.8%). In comparison, the C2+ selectivity of P-GDE decreases (Fig. S26 and Table S3 in the ESM), showing FEC2H4 of 6.6% ± 5.2% and FEC2H5OH of 20.1% ± 8.7% at j of 300 mA·cm−2, which are lower than those of H-GDE (30.3% ± 3.5% for C2H4 and 29.1% ± 3.3% for C2H5OH). Even worse, the P-GDE without hydrophobic treatment on the catalyst layer could not sustain steady high current density (e.g., 500 mA·cm−2, Fig. 1(c)). The total C2+ FEs of H-GDE surpass those of P-GDE, which benefits from the abundant three-phase interfaces (Fig. 3(d)). In addition, the C2+ half-cell energy conversion efficiency (ECE) was calculated [25, 37]. The H-GDE could motivate CO2RR at a high ECE of 40.4% ± 4.4%, and maintain over 30.0% ECE ranging from 100 to 800 mA·cm−2, which shows higher ECEs than the P-GDE (Fig. 3(c) and Fig. S26 in the ESM). The formation rates of C2+ products on H-GDE have reached 2,206.5 ± 152 μmol·h−1·cm−2 at a j of 800 mA·cm−2 (Fig. 3(e)), which shows a huge potential for future industrial application at high-current level. These above performance analysis results show that the hydrophobic treatment over the catalyst layer would significantly promote the CO2 gas diffusion electrolysis both in C2+ selectivity and catalytic current densities. The long-term CO2 gas diffusion electrolysis test was undertaken in 1.0 M KOH electrolyte to evaluate the stability of the GDEs. In Fig. S1 in the ESM, the hydrophobic molecular functionalized GDE could sustain the continuous electrolysis at the j of 100 mA·cm−2 for more than 40 h, without obvious degradation at the applied potential.
In order to further verify the availability of hydrophobic molecular engineering strategy for improving the stability of GDE, we chose another more stable GDL of Sigracet 28 BC instead of H14C9 as the electrode substrate. Using the same hydrophobic treatment, a more stable hydrophobic GDE was obtained (namely S-H-GDE). S-H-GDE could maintain stable CO2RR at 200 mA·cm−2 for more than 100 h without flooding (Fig. 4). The selectivity of C2+ keeps at approximately 65% even after 80 h (Table S4 in the ESM). In contrast, the S-P-GDE without hydrophobic treatment suffers from obvious flooding soon (Figs. S27 and S28 in the ESM), which strongly confirms the effectiveness of hydrophobic molecular functionalization.
Until now, a great deal of works for stable CO2RR at relatively high current densities have been reported. However, few of them could achieve long-term stability (over 50 h) for CO2RR at > 100 mA∙cm−2, most of which were undertaken in neutral electrolyte, or directly used fibrous PTFE as GDL (Table S5 in the ESM). This work paves a new avenue for sustaining stable high-current CO2RR in an aqueous flow cell using carbonbased GDLs.

sections.heading: 4 Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, the hydrophobic molecular was functionalized over the Cu catalyst layer of the GDE, which significantly promotes the activity and stability for CO2 gas diffusion electrolysis. The 1-octadecanethiol modified Cu catalyst layer on the GDE could deliver high-current electrolysis without flooding, and exhibit high C2+ FEs over 70.0% in the j ranging from 100 to 800 mA∙cm−2, with the peak FEC2+ of 85.2% at 800 mA∙cm−2. The anchored hydrophobic molecular layer would continuously and roundly functionalize the catalyst layer with hydrophobicity, which extends the solid–liquid–gas three-phase interfaces inside the catalyst layer instead of the

This hydrophobic molecular engineering strategy over the GDE shortens the CO2 gas diffusion length, concentrates the CO2 over the catalyst, and prevents the GDL from flooding. We believe other cathodic reactions can benefit from this study with aim to promote activity and selectivity for long-term high-current gas diffusion electrolysis.
